what: Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte operates airports in Mexico. It holds long-term concessions to run thirteen airports, the largest being Monterrey, and earns money from airlines using the runways and from passengers using the terminals — plus the shops, car parks and hotels inside them.
customers: Airlines paying landing and passenger charges, and the passengers who shop, eat, park and stay in hotels at its airports.
money: Regulated charges per passenger and per aircraft movement, set under the concession.
Retail, food, car parking, advertising and hotel revenue, at much higher margins.
moat: An airport concession is a legal monopoly for decades: no one else may operate that airport, and nobody is building a competing one next to Monterrey. Charges are regulated but set in a formula that allows a return on invested capital, and the commercial revenue inside the terminal is unregulated — which is why the shops matter more to profit than the runways.
risks: Mexican aviation regulation changed abruptly in recent years when the government cut the allowed maximum tariffs, which shows how much is outside the company’s control.
Revenue swung from $854.5M in 2023 to $725.1M in 2024, partly reflecting those tariff changes and currency.
Monterrey’s industrial economy drives much of the traffic, so a manufacturing slowdown reduces passengers.
The share price is in dollars while earnings are in pesos, so currency alone changes the return for a foreign holder.
Only seven analysts cover the stock, so the $117.13 average target rests on thin coverage.
opportunities: Last year’s net margin was 33.5%, which is exceptional and reflects the monopoly nature of the asset.
Free cash flow of $337.8M on $913.1M of revenue, at about 14.8 times free cash flow and 10.4 times EV/EBITDA.
Concessions run for decades and cannot be competed against — nobody builds a second Monterrey airport.
Commercial revenue inside the terminal is unregulated and grows faster than passenger charges.
Nearshoring of manufacturing to northern Mexico is a genuine structural driver of traffic through Monterrey.
watch: Passenger traffic growth and commercial revenue per passenger. Traffic drives the regulated revenue; what each passenger spends inside the terminal drives the profit.
view: Airports are among the best assets in the world and it is worth being clear why. The concession is a legal monopoly for decades, nobody can build a competing airport next to an existing one, and demand grows with population and income over very long periods. A 33.5% net margin is what that looks like in the accounts, and it is not a cyclical artefact — it is the nature of owning the only runway in a major city.

The commercial revenue is where the value compounds. Passenger and aircraft charges are regulated, set under a formula that allows a return on invested capital, so there is a ceiling on them. The shops, restaurants, car parks and advertising inside the terminal are not regulated, and revenue per passenger from those can rise indefinitely as traffic grows and the offer improves. That is the half of the business worth tracking.

The specific driver for Monterrey is more interesting than general traffic growth. Northern Mexico has been the main beneficiary of manufacturing moving out of China toward North America, and Monterrey is its industrial centre. That brings business travellers, air cargo and the economic growth that generates leisure travel — a structural tailwind rather than a cyclical one.

What keeps the multiple at 10.4 times EV/EBITDA is Mexican regulatory risk, and it is not theoretical: the government cut the allowed maximum tariffs at these airports in recent years, which directly reduced revenue. A regulated monopoly is only as good as the regulator’s restraint, and Mexican policy has shown it can move abruptly. Add currency — earnings in pesos, share price in dollars — and you have a wonderful asset at a discount for reasons that are real and recurring. Traffic and commercial revenue per passenger are the numbers.
bull: Nearshoring keeps driving Monterrey traffic while unregulated commercial revenue per passenger compounds on a decades-long monopoly concession.
bear: Mexican regulators cut allowed tariffs again, a manufacturing slowdown reduces traffic, and peso weakness erases the dollar investor’s return.
